title: What should you ask first in a pricing case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a pricing case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Pricing cases have no single right answer, which can feel unsettling. Here is how to reach a sensible number and defend it.
body:
The first question to ask

What is the product worth to the customer?

How to build your structure

  • Floor: variable cost per unit, fixed costs to recover
  • Ceiling: value to the customer, price of their next best option
  • Reference: competitor prices, substitutes
  • Choose: penetration or skimming, volume at each price, effect on our other products

The trap most people fall into

Using only one lens; no volume assumption.

For the full tree, with every branch, read the pricing framework.

Two prompts to try

Should a streaming service launch a cheaper plan with ads?

Show a model structure
  • New subscribers: People who find the full price too high; Win-back of those who left
  • Downgrades: Current subscribers switching to cheaper plan; Revenue lost per switch
  • Ad revenue: Ads per hour, price advertisers pay; Viewer experience
  • Capability: Ad sales team, technology; Content rights for ads

Where to start: Downgrades: ad revenue must make up for subscribers who switch down.

The trap: Counting only the new subscribers.

Test the proposed increase against lost volume

A cinema charges £10 per ticket. The incremental cost of serving another visitor is £3, so contribution is £7. It currently sells 100,000 tickets, generating £700,000 of contribution before fixed costs. Management proposes raising the ticket price to £12.

At £12, contribution is £9 per ticket. Break-even volume relative to the old contribution is £700,000 ÷ £9 ≈ 77,800 tickets. That means the business could lose about 22% of its tickets and still maintain the old contribution, assuming the per-visitor variable cost is unchanged and other income does not move.

But cinemas also earn food and drink margins, so losing attendance could hurt more than ticket economics suggest. Check willingness to pay by customer segment, competitor prices, off-peak utilisation and the possibility of testing different prices by day. A strong price recommendation specifies how to test demand, not merely the arithmetic.
